>Unit 4: Transport

SKILLS FOCUS: Listening

You will hear an audio text and respond to it by filling in gaps in multiple-choice questions, to show your understanding of what you have heard.

LEARNING INTENTIONS

By the end of this unit you will be able to:
  • understand and use a range of vocabulary related to the topic of transport
  • communicate information, ideas and opinions in a discussion about a particular form of transport
  • show understanding of the ideas and attitudes expressed by people talking about their travel and transport experiences
  • understand and use the passive voice
  • communicate surprise in speech clearly and effectively, and contribute to a group discussion.

BSpeaking and vocabulary
4Work in groups. Discuss the following questions about the methods of transport from Activity B3.
aWhich of them have you used?
bWhich was the most enjoyable? Why? Which was the least enjoyable?
cWhich would you like to use? Why?
dWhat do you think are the advantages and disadvantages of each method?
Example: A high-speed train is fast but expensive.
a — sample answer
a I’ve used the underground, ferries and coaches, but I’ve never been in a helicopter.
b — sample answer
b The ferry was the most enjoyable – the sea views were beautiful. The least enjoyable was a long coach journey: slow and uncomfortable.
c — sample answer
c I’d like to try a hot-air balloon because the views would be amazing.
d — sample answer
d A bicycle is cheap and healthy, but slow in the rain. A plane is fast, but it’s bad for the environment.

BSpeaking and vocabulary
5Work in groups of three. Each person should choose one of the three topics below and write three notes about it. One example is given for each topic.
aThe problems with different methods of transport
Example: air pollution
Sample notes
  • traffic jams in big cities
  • accidents on busy roads
  • delays and cancellations
  • tickets can be expensive
bHow transport has changed in your lifetime
Example: too much traffic in town centres
Sample notes
  • more electric scooters and cars
  • ride-hailing apps (e.g. Grab)
  • new metro lines
  • tickets bought on your phone
cThe future of transport
Example: less air travel
Sample notes
  • driverless cars and buses
  • flying taxis
  • faster high-speed trains
  • more people cycling or walking

Text 4.1

[1] While airships may appear in a few recent novels and films, the (a) . . . reality is that they are few and far between in the modern world. Some can be seen occasionally in the skies above the USA, advertising a product and perhaps carrying a few passengers. A few more are sometimes seen on a tourist outing in parts of Europe.

[2] But if airship enthusiasts are to be believed, in the next few years the enormous Airlander airship will be the first to fly to the North Pole since 1928. Each tourist on board will have to pay $80 000 for this luxury experience, and tickets are already being sold.

[3] The Airlander will accommodate up to 16 passengers and eight crew in the 200-square-metre main cabin. The cabin arrangement can be changed, but the focus is always on (b) . . . comfort and safety – and on offering as many opportunities as possible to see the (c) . . . breathtaking views through the glass windows and floor. The airship can travel up to about 3700 km without stopping, and could stay in the sky for three days at a height of just under 5 km.

[4] At about the same time, an enormous new airship in the shape of a blue whale will take to the skies. This one is not being built for tourism, but for lifting heavy machines and equipment in some of the (d) . . . toughest landscapes on the planet. It is 150 metres long (about the same as an A380 plane) and just as high, made up of 12 (e) . . . storeys. Eventually, these two may not be the only new airships. Nowadays, there seems to be increasing demand for engineers and pilots in an industry that everyone thought was finished.

CReading
4Now read the text in more detail. Discuss these questions in pairs.
aWhich piece of information in the text surprised you most? Why?
a — sample answer
I was surprised that a ticket costs $80 000 – and they are already being sold!
bWould you like to travel in an airship? Why, or why not?
b — sample answers
Yes – the views through the glass floor would be breathtaking. No – it’s slow and very expensive.
cWhat do you think are the advantages and disadvantages of this method of transport?
c — some ideas
+ quiet, amazing views, can stay up for days, can lift heavy machines to difficult places
– slow, very expensive, few airships, bad weather and wind can be a problem
Text 4.1 · p. 52 (completed)

[1] While airships may appear in a few recent novels and films, the reality is that they are few and far between in the modern world. Some can be seen occasionally in the skies above the USA, advertising a product and perhaps carrying a few passengers. A few more are sometimes seen on a tourist outing in parts of Europe.

[2] But if airship enthusiasts are to be believed, in the next few years the enormous Airlander airship will be the first to fly to the North Pole since 1928. Each tourist on board will have to pay $80 000 for this luxury experience, and tickets are already being sold.

[3] The Airlander will accommodate up to 16 passengers and eight crew in the 200-square-metre main cabin. The cabin arrangement can be changed, but the focus is always on comfort and safety – and on offering as many opportunities as possible to see the breathtaking views through the glass windows and floor. The airship can travel up to about 3700 km without stopping, and could stay in the sky for three days at a height of just under 5 km.

[4] At about the same time, an enormous new airship in the shape of a blue whale will take to the skies. This one is not being built for tourism, but for lifting heavy machines and equipment in some of the toughest landscapes on the planet. It is 150 metres long (about the same as an A380 plane) and just as high, made up of 12 storeys. Eventually, these two may not be the only new airships. Nowadays, there seems to be increasing demand for engineers and pilots in an industry that everyone thought was finished.
